learn.taste: Red cherry, dried herbs and a smoky, flinty edge. Light to medium body with fine but firm tannins.
learn.why: The vines grow on the slopes of an active volcano, some above 1,000 metres. The altitude keeps acidity high, and the black volcanic soils give the smoky, mineral streak.
learn.label: Look for 'Etna Rosso DOC'. Nerello Mascalese is the main grape, often with a little Nerello Cappuccio.
learn.ask: Something like a Pinot Noir or Nebbiolo but more mineral: do you have an Etna Rosso?

learn.taste: Black cherry, plum, tar and smoke, with powerful tannins and fresh acidity.
learn.why: Aglianico ripens late on volcanic soils, so it keeps high acidity alongside big tannins. That combination makes it one of Italy's longest-lived reds.
learn.label: 'Taurasi DOCG' and 'Aglianico del Vulture' are the classic names. Younger, cheaper bottles just say 'Aglianico'.
learn.ask: I'd like something big and structured. Is there an Aglianico or a Taurasi on the list?

name: Northern Rhône Syrah
adds: black pepper, olive and smoked-meat notes

learn.taste: Blackberry, black pepper, olive and smoky, meaty notes. Medium to full body with firm tannins.
learn.why: The cooler Northern Rhône gives Syrah a peppery, savoury style, very different from riper Australian Shiraz. The pepper comes from a compound called rotundone.
learn.label: Crozes-Hermitage and Saint-Joseph are the affordable way in; Côte-Rôtie, Hermitage and Cornas are the top names. They're all Syrah, though the grape is rarely on the label.
learn.ask: I'd like a Northern Rhône Syrah: a Crozes-Hermitage or a Saint-Joseph.

learn.taste: Dark plum, blackberry and violets, with firm tannins and a full body.
learn.why: It's the same steep valley and the same grapes that make Port, fermented dry instead of fortified. Tinta Roriz is the local name for Tempranillo.
learn.label: Look for 'Douro DOC', with Touriga Nacional named on the back label.
learn.ask: Do you have a dry red from the Douro?

name: Cru Beaujolais
adds: juicy, floral fruit at a friendly price

learn.taste: Crunchy red cherry, raspberry and violets. Light body, low tannin and fresh acidity.
learn.why: Gamay grown on granite in the ten Beaujolais 'crus' makes far more serious wine than Beaujolais Nouveau, and the best age like lighter Burgundy.
learn.label: Look for a village name rather than just 'Beaujolais': Morgon, Fleurie, Moulin-à-Vent or Brouilly.
learn.ask: Something light and fresh, like a Morgon or a Fleurie?

learn.taste: Sour cherry, plum and a juicy, mouth-watering finish, with very gentle tannins.
learn.why: Barbera is naturally high in acid but low in tannin, which makes it one of Italy's most food-friendly everyday reds.
learn.label: The grape is in the name: 'Barbera d'Asti' or 'Barbera d'Alba'.
learn.ask: A Barbera for the table, something fresh to go with the food.

learn.taste: Red and black fruit, violets, a hint of pepper and slate. Medium body with fresh acidity.
learn.why: Grown on steep slate slopes in north-west Spain, Mencía sits somewhere between Pinot Noir and Cabernet Franc in style.
learn.label: Look for 'Bierzo DO' or 'Ribeira Sacra'. Mencía is usually named on the label.
learn.ask: Do you have a Mencía from Bierzo or Ribeira Sacra?

name: High-altitude Malbec
adds: plush dark fruit with a violet lift

learn.taste: Blackberry, plum, cocoa and violet. Full body with smooth, medium tannins.
learn.why: Vineyards up to 1,500 metres in the Andes get intense sun but cold nights, giving deep colour and ripe fruit that still tastes fresh.
learn.label: 'Mendoza' or a sub-region like 'Uco Valley' or 'Luján de Cuyo', with Malbec on the front label.
learn.ask: A Malbec from the Uco Valley, if you have one.

learn.taste: Raspberry, red pepper and pencil shavings. Medium body and fresh.
learn.why: Cabernet Franc is a parent of Cabernet Sauvignon. In the cool Loire it's lighter and more herbal than in Bordeaux blends.
learn.label: Chinon, Bourgueil and Saumur-Champigny are Loire Cabernet Franc, though the grape rarely appears on the label.
learn.ask: I'd like to try a Chinon or another Loire Cabernet Franc.

learn.taste: Green apple, lime, white pepper and a savoury, lentil-like note. Crisp and dry.
learn.why: Austria's signature grape. Its peppery note comes from rotundone, the same compound that makes Syrah peppery.
learn.label: Grüner Veltliner is on the label. Wachau wines are graded Steinfeder, Federspiel and Smaragd, from lightest to richest.
learn.ask: Something crisp and dry, like a Grüner Veltliner?

learn.taste: Lemon, sea salt and flint. Bone dry with searing acidity and surprising weight.
learn.why: Santorini's vines are trained into low baskets called 'kouloura' to shelter the grapes from the wind. Volcanic soil and sea air give the salty edge.
learn.label: 'Santorini PDO' on the label means Assyrtiko.
learn.ask: Do you have an Assyrtiko from Santorini?

learn.taste: Peach, lemon and a salty tang. Light and zesty.
learn.why: Grown in rainy, Atlantic-facing Galicia, often on high pergolas to keep air around the grapes, which keeps it fresh and aromatic.
learn.label: 'Rías Baixas' and 'Albariño'. Over the border in Portugal the same grape is Alvarinho, in Vinho Verde.
learn.ask: A crisp coastal white, like an Albariño from Rías Baixas.

name: Chenin Blanc
adds: honeyed apple and a waxy richness

learn.taste: Quince, baked apple, honey and chamomile. It can be dry, off-dry or sweet.
learn.why: Chenin's high acidity lets it be made in every style, from dry to sweet to sparkling. Vouvray labels say 'sec' (dry), 'demi-sec' (off-dry) or 'moelleux' (sweet).
learn.label: Vouvray or Savennières in the Loire, or 'Chenin Blanc' from South Africa's Swartland and Stellenbosch.
learn.ask: Do you have a dry Chenin Blanc? A Vouvray sec or something from South Africa?

learn.taste: Green apple, lemon and oyster shell. Little or no oak, and taut.
learn.why: Chablis is Chardonnay grown on limestone full of fossilised oyster shells, in Burgundy's coolest corner.
learn.label: Plain 'Chablis', then 'Premier Cru' and 'Grand Cru' for single vineyards.
learn.ask: I'd like an unoaked Chardonnay. Is there a Chablis?

learn.taste: Lime, green apple and wet slate, with very high acidity. The best age for decades, picking up honeyed and petrol notes.
learn.why: The steep slate slopes of the Mosel reflect heat onto the vines. 'Trocken' on the label means dry.
learn.label: 'Trocken' means dry. 'Kabinett' is lighter and often off-dry. 'Grosses Gewächs' (GG) are the top dry wines.
learn.ask: A dry Riesling, a Trocken from the Mosel or Rheingau.

learn.taste: Apricot, peach and honeysuckle. Full and rich, with low acidity.
learn.why: Condrieu in the Northern Rhône is Viognier's home. The grape almost vanished in the 1960s before being revived.
learn.label: Condrieu for the classic, or 'Viognier' from the Languedoc, California or Australia.
learn.ask: Something rich and aromatic. Do you have a Viognier?

learn.taste: Strawberry, raspberry and spice. Fuller and darker than Provence rosé.
learn.why: Tavel is France's only appellation that makes nothing but rosé. Longer skin contact gives it colour and grip.
learn.label: 'Tavel AOC' on the label.
learn.ask: A rosé with some weight to it. Do you have a Tavel?

learn.taste: Red fruit, orange peel, herbs and a salty minerality. Dry and structured.
learn.why: Mourvèdre needs Bandol's hot, sea-facing slopes to ripen. Bandol rosé ages better than most.
learn.label: 'Bandol AOC' on the label.
learn.ask: A more serious dry rosé, like a Bandol.

learn.taste: Watermelon, strawberry and cherry. Fruity and bright.
learn.why: Navarra built its name on Garnacha rosado, made by giving red grapes a short time on their skins.
learn.label: 'Navarra DO' and 'rosado'.
learn.ask: A fruity Spanish rosado, from Navarra if you have one.

name: Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo
adds: cherry depth between rosé and light red

learn.taste: Cherry, blood orange and herbs. A deep cherry-coloured rosé with some grip.
learn.why: Cerasuolo means 'cherry-red'. It's made from Montepulciano and sits somewhere between rosé and a light red.
learn.label: 'Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo DOC' on the label.
learn.ask: A darker, food-friendly rosé, like a Cerasuolo d'Abruzzo.

name: Crémant
adds: the Champagne method at a fraction of the price

learn.taste: Apple, citrus and a light brioche note, with fine bubbles.
learn.why: Crémant uses the same traditional method as Champagne, a second fermentation in the bottle, but comes from other French regions.
learn.label: 'Crémant de Bourgogne', 'Crémant de Loire' or 'Crémant d'Alsace'.
learn.ask: Something like Champagne but better value. Do you have a Crémant?

learn.taste: Ripe apple, almond and brioche, with a creamy mousse.
learn.why: Italy's top traditional-method sparkling. It must spend at least 18 months ageing on its lees.
learn.label: 'Franciacorta DOCG' on the label.
learn.ask: An Italian traditional-method sparkling. Is there a Franciacorta?

learn.taste: Green apple, lemon and hedgerow flowers. Very fresh.
learn.why: Southern England's chalk is part of the same geological seam as Champagne's, and the cool climate gives very high acidity.
learn.label: Look for Sussex, Kent or Hampshire. Most use Champagne's three grapes.
learn.ask: Do you have an English sparkling wine?

name: Cava Reserva
adds: a savoury, toasty edge from long ageing

learn.taste: Lemon, apple, almond and a savoury, toasty note.
learn.why: Cava is made by the traditional method. Reserva spends at least 18 months on its lees and Gran Reserva 30, which builds the toastiness.
learn.label: 'Cava' plus 'Reserva' or 'Gran Reserva'. Some top growers now label as 'Corpinnat'.
learn.ask: A Cava with some age on it, a Reserva or Gran Reserva.

learn.taste: Fresh fruit, a little yeastiness and gentle, sometimes cloudy bubbles.
learn.why: Pétillant naturel is bottled before its first fermentation finishes, so the bubbles come from that one fermentation. It's the oldest way of making sparkling wine.
learn.label: 'Pét-Nat', 'Pétillant Naturel' or 'Méthode Ancestrale' on the label.
learn.ask: Do you have a Pét-Nat? I'd like to try something different.

name: Georgian Qvevri Amber
adds: the ancient original of skin-contact wine

learn.taste: Dried apricot, orange peel, walnut and tea, with real tannic grip.
learn.why: Georgia has made wine in buried clay jars called qvevri for around 8,000 years. White grapes ferment on their skins for months.
learn.label: 'Qvevri' or 'Kakheti' on the label, with Rkatsiteli or Mtsvane.
learn.ask: Do you have a Georgian qvevri wine?

name: Ramato Pinot Grigio
adds: a lighter, copper-hued take on skin contact

learn.taste: Pear, red apple, spice and a light grip. Copper-pink in the glass.
learn.why: Pinot Grigio has pinkish-grey skins. A short time on the skins gives 'ramato' (copper) its colour, the traditional Venetian way to make it.
learn.label: 'Ramato' on the label, usually from Friuli.
learn.ask: Do you have a ramato Pinot Grigio?

name: Macerated Ribolla Gialla
adds: the modern classic of skin-contact whites

learn.taste: Dried apricot, honey, herbs and firm tannins, with bright acidity.
learn.why: In the 1990s growers in Collio, on the Italy–Slovenia border, revived long skin contact inspired by Georgian qvevri wines.
learn.label: Collio (Italy) or Brda (Slovenia), with Ribolla Gialla (Rebula in Slovenian).
learn.ask: Is there a skin-contact Ribolla Gialla on the list?

learn.taste: Apricot, honey, marmalade and saffron. Rich and luscious, with enough acidity to stay fresh.
learn.why: Autumn mists encourage 'noble rot', a fungus that shrivels the grapes and concentrates their sugar and acid.
learn.label: Sauternes or neighbouring Barsac.
learn.ask: A glass of Sauternes with dessert, please.

name: Tokaji Aszú
adds: sweetness with a searing, lively acidity

learn.taste: Apricot, orange peel, honey and tea. Intensely sweet but vivid.
learn.why: Aszú berries are shrivelled by noble rot and added to base wine. 'Puttonyos' on older labels measures how sweet it is.
learn.label: 'Tokaji Aszú', often with 5 or 6 puttonyos.
learn.ask: Do you have a Tokaji Aszú?

name: Riesling Auslese
adds: lighter sweetness balanced by piercing acidity

learn.taste: Peach, lime, honey and slate. Sweet but light and low in alcohol.
learn.why: German Prädikat levels measure grape ripeness at harvest: Kabinett, Spätlese, Auslese, then Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese.
learn.label: 'Auslese' or 'Spätlese' on a German Riesling label.
learn.ask: A sweet Riesling, like an Auslese from the Mosel.

learn.taste: Grape, peach, orange blossom. Gently sparkling, sweet and only about 5% alcohol.
learn.why: Fermentation is stopped early, leaving natural grape sugar and a soft fizz.
learn.label: 'Moscato d'Asti DOCG'.
learn.ask: Something light and sweet with dessert, like a Moscato d'Asti.

learn.taste: Almond, bread dough, green apple and sea salt. Bone dry and light.
learn.why: It ages under a layer of yeast called 'flor', which protects it from oxygen and gives the salty, bready tang. Manzanilla is Fino aged by the sea in Sanlúcar.
learn.label: 'Fino' or 'Manzanilla' on the label. Serve chilled, and drink within a few days of opening.
learn.ask: A chilled glass of Fino or Manzanilla, please.

name: Amontillado Sherry
adds: a nutty depth from two kinds of ageing

learn.taste: Hazelnut, caramel, orange peel and a savoury finish. Dry.
learn.why: It starts ageing under flor like a Fino, then the flor dies away and it ages in contact with air, turning amber and nutty.
learn.label: 'Amontillado' on the label. Check it says dry ('seco') if you want the classic style.
learn.ask: Do you have a dry Amontillado?

learn.taste: Dried fig, caramel, walnut and orange peel. Sweet and mellow.
learn.why: Aged for years in small casks, where slow exposure to air turns its colour tawny and trades fresh fruit for nutty flavours.
learn.label: '10 Year Old Tawny' (or 20, 30, 40) on the label.
learn.ask: A glass of 10-year tawny Port.

learn.taste: Caramel, toffee, citrus peel and walnut, always with a tangy acidity.
learn.why: Madeira is deliberately heated as it ages, so it barely changes once opened. Sercial is the driest style, then Verdelho, Bual and Malmsey, the sweetest.
learn.label: The grape on the label tells you the sweetness: Sercial, Verdelho, Bual or Malmsey.
learn.ask: Do you have a Madeira? A Bual or Verdelho, perhaps?
